name: Abaddon
title: Angel of the Abyss – Prince of Destruction
summary: Abaddon (Hebrew: אֲבַדּוֹן, 'destruction') is a biblical concept that appears in two fundamentally different functions throughout Scripture. In the wisdom literature of the Old Testament, the name denotes the deepest and most destructive realm of the underworld – the place of perdition that nonetheless lies naked and open to God's all-seeing gaze (Job 26:6; Prov 15:11; Ps 88:12). Sheol and Abaddon consistently appear in poetic parallelism to express death's insatiable greed (Prov 27:20), while Job 28:22 portrays Abaddon and death as witnesses who have only heard the rumor of God's inaccessible wisdom. In Revelation 9:11, the concept undergoes a radical transformation: Abaddon now appears as a named, personified angel over the abyss (Greek: ἄβυσσος), the ruler over locust-like creatures released under the judgment of the fifth trumpet. John also cites the Greek equivalent Apollyon ('the destroyer'), a designation that may contain a polemical edge against the Greco-Roman god Apollo – central to Emperor Domitian's self-presentation. The movement from an abstract place-concept in wisdom literature to an apocalyptic ruler in Revelation reflects the marked development in Jewish cosmology during the intertestamental period, visible in texts such as the Hodayot from Qumran and other apocalyptic writings. Theologically, Abaddon reveals that destructive and death-bringing forces do not operate autonomously, but remain subject to God's sovereign will and serve as instruments in his judgment over a rebellious world.
roles: King over the creatures of the abyss

keyEvents.title: Abaddon as the deepest place in the realm of the dead in the Book of Job
keyEvents.description: In the Book of Job, Abaddon is mentioned repeatedly as a term for the place of destruction in the afterlife. Job 26:6 declares that Sheol (the realm of the dead) lies naked before God and Abaddon without cover, an expression of God's all-encompassing insight. In Job 28:22, Abaddon and death are personified as witnesses who have heard the rumor of God's wisdom but never fully grasped it. Job 31:12 uses Abaddon as a metaphor for total destruction—a consuming fire that burns all the way down to Abaddon.

keyEvents.title: Abaddon in the Book of Psalms
keyEvents.description: In Psalm 88:12, the psalmist poses the rhetorical question whether God's faithfulness is proclaimed in Abaddon—the place of destruction among the dead. The question underscores the silence of the dead and the psalmist's deep despair, suggesting that Abaddon is a place beyond the reach of praise.

keyEvents.title: Abaddon in Proverbs
keyEvents.description: Proverbs uses Abaddon alongside Sheol to highlight God's omniscience and the insatiable nature of death. Proverbs 15:11 states that Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the Lord—how much more then the hearts of people. Proverbs 27:20 compares the insatiable maw of Abaddon and Sheol to the greediness of human eyes.

keyEvents.title: The Angel of the Abyss and the judgment of the fifth trumpet
keyEvents.description: In John's Revelation, Abaddon is explicitly identified as the angel over the abyss (ἄβυσσος) and the king over locust-like creatures that rise up under the judgment of the fifth trumpet. The abyss is opened with a key, smoke rises like from a great furnace, and the creatures are given power to torment people who do not have God's seal for five months. In verse 11 their king is named: in Hebrew Abaddon, in Greek Apollyon – the destroyer. This is the only place in the Bible where Abaddon appears as a personified, named apocalyptic figure with an active ruling function.

versions.summary: Abaddon is a name found in the Bible, meaning 'destruction' or 'perdition'. In the Old Testament, the name is used as a term for the deepest abyss of the realm of the dead, while in Revelation 9:11, Abaddon appears as the angel over the abyss, also called Apollyon in Greek. The figure symbolizes destruction and judgment and is linked to end-time prophecies.

versions.reason: [major] Abaddon is not primarily associated with the 'early-church' era. Although the name appears in Revelation (written in the early church period), it also occurs in the OT (Job, Psalms, Proverbs). As an apocalyptic/supernatural figure without a defined historical time period, and because Revelation deals with the end times, 'early-church' could be defended since Revelation was written then. But the concept extends throughout the entire Bible. Nevertheless, 'early-church' is retained because Rev 9:11 contains the central personification.; [major] The roles array is empty. Abaddon should have roles describing his function, e.g., 'Angel of the Abyss', 'Destroyer', etc.; [minor] The title 'Angel of Destruction' is good but could be refined to 'Angel of the Abyss and Destroyer' to capture both aspects – the place designation in the OT and the personified angel in Revelation.; [minor] The last two key events ('Judgment of the Fifth Trumpet' and 'The King of the Abyss in Revelation') overlap significantly in both content and biblical references (Rev 9:1-11). They could be merged into a single event to avoid redundancy.; [minor] Job 31:12 mentions 'Abaddon' in some translations, but in many translations the word 'destruction' is used without directly referring to Abaddon as a place/person. The reference is acceptable but should be verified against the Hebrew original – the Hebrew word here is actually 'abaddoh' (a form of abaddon), so it can be defended.; [major] No footnotes are included. A profile on Abaddon should include footnotes on etymology, the relationship to Greek Apollyon, rabbinic interpretations, and possible connections to Greco-Roman mythology (Apollo).; [minor] The lifespan field is missing. For a supernatural/symbolic figure this is expected to be empty but should explicitly be set to an appropriate value.; [minor] The summary is good but could mention the dual nature: place designation in the OT versus personified angel in the NT, even more clearly and with reference to the Hebrew etymology (אֲבַדּוֹן).

versions.summary: Abaddon (Hebrew: אֲבַדּוֹן, 'destruction') appears in the Bible in two fundamentally different ways. In the wisdom literature of the Old Testament, the name functions as a designation for the deepest and most destructive sphere of the realm of the dead – a place of ruin and perdition that nonetheless lies open and naked before God's all-knowing gaze (Job 26:6; Prov 15:11; Ps 88:12). Sheol and Abaddon often appear in poetic parallelism to emphasize the insatiable nature of death (Prov 27:20). In Revelation 9:11, the concept undergoes a dramatic transformation: Abaddon is personified as the angel over the abyss, the ruler over the locust-like creatures that rise up under the judgment of the fifth trumpet. John also gives the Greek equivalent Apollyon ('the destroyer'), possibly with polemical edge against the Greco-Roman god Apollo. This transition from an abstract place-concept in the OT to a named apocalyptic figure in the NT reflects the development in Jewish cosmology from wisdom literature through the intertestamental period to early Christian apocalypticism. Theologically, Abaddon represents God's destructive judgment and illustrates that even destructive forces operate within the framework of God's sovereign will.
versions.title: Angel of the Abyss – Prince of Destruction
versions.reason: [minor] Abaddon appears primarily in Old Testament wisdom literature (Job, Psalms, Proverbs) and only once in the New Testament (Revelation). Assigning the era to 'early-church' is not directly incorrect since Revelation is where the personification occurs, but it may be misleading given that most biblical texts about Abaddon belong to the wisdom literature period. Since this is a supernatural/symbolic figure spanning multiple eras, the choice is nevertheless defensible enough.; [minor] In the sentence 'From an abstract place concept in the OT', a 'n' is missing – it should read 'place concept' → 'place concept'. Actually, 'place concept' is correct enough as a compound word, but it could be made clearer as 'place concept' or 'location concept'. The correction is trivial.; [minor] The description of the judgment of the fifth trumpet is very detailed and good, but it might be worth explicitly mentioning that 'the abyss' (Greek: ἄβυσσος/abyssos) is a key term linking the text to the Old Testament concept. This is already partially covered in the footnotes, but could strengthen the description.; [minor] The footnote about the Dead Sea Scrolls (4Q491 and Hodayot) is marked as 'archaeological', which is reasonable, but the reference could have been more precise. 4Q491 (War Scroll fragment) does not mention Abaddon directly; Hodayot (1QHa) is a better reference for the concept of Abaddon in Qumran texts. In fact, it is 1QHa xi (formerly iii) that explicitly mentions 'Abaddon'.

footnotes.text: In the Hebrew text of 1QHa (Hodayot/T Thanksgiving Hymns) from Qumran, the word Abaddon appears several times, including in column xi, where the author describes his deliverance from 'the gates of Sheol' and 'the streams of Abaddon'. This confirms that the concept was actively used in Jewish theology during the intertestamental period and contributed to the development of the abyss concept found in Revelation.

The transition from Abaddon as a place name to a personified figure reflects a broader trend in Jewish apocalyptic literature in the last century BCE and the first century CE, where cosmic places and powers were increasingly personified and given names. This development is clearly seen in texts such as 1 Enoch, the Book of Jubilees, and the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs.

The Hebrew verb אָבַד (ʾāḇaḏ) appears over 180 times in the OT and covers a broad semantic range from 'to go astray' to 'to perish' and 'to be destroyed'. The noun אֲבַדּוֹן represents an intensive form that emphasizes total and final destruction – making it a fitting name for both the deepest realm of the dead and an apocalyptic destroyer figure.
